opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few reasons it's such a natural fit. The first is that interpretability research is, at its core, an incredibly iterative, empirical loop. You form a hypothesis about what some feature or circuit is doing, you design an experiment — maybe an ablation, maybe activation patching, maybe looking at top-activating examples — you run it, you look at the results, and then you refine the hypothesis. That loop is exactly the kind of thing agents are getting really good at. It's mostly code, it's mostly running things and reading outputs, and the feedback is relatively fast.

The second thing is scale. Modern models have millions, sometimes billions, of features once you decompose them with something like sparse autoencoders. No team of human researchers is ever going to look at all of those carefully. So if we want interpretability to actually keep pace with the models we're deploying, we need some way to scale up the investigative labor itself, not just the compute. Agents give you that — you can spin up many of them in parallel, each chasing down a different feature or behavior.

Third, a lot of interpretability work is honestly kind of tedious in ways that don't require deep insight at every step. Writing the hooks, sweeping over layers, generating contrastive prompts, labeling examples — these are things where a capable agent can do eighty or ninety percent of the grunt work, and then the human researcher can focus on the parts that really need judgment: is this explanation actually right, is it capturing the mechanism or just a correlation, what's the next big question.

And then there's a nice property that the ground truth is, in some sense, available. Unlike a lot of science where you're limited by what you can measure in the world, with a neural network you have full access to every weight and every activation. You can intervene anywhere. So an agent can actually test its claims causally and get a definitive answer, which makes it much easier to verify whether the agent is doing good work or just telling a plausible story.

That last point is important, because the big risk is that agents produce explanations that sound convincing but aren't faithful. So a lot of what we think about is how to build the tooling and the evaluation around agents so that their findings are grounded in causal evidence rather than just pattern-matching on what an interpretability paper is supposed to look like.

r001.rationale: The response describes interpretability as an iterative empirical loop of forming hypotheses, running experiments, reviewing results, and refining hypotheses.

r002.rationale: It says modern models have millions or billions of features and that no human research team can inspect them all carefully, communicating that their scale exceeds human capacity to encompass them.

r003.rationale: It says agents can work in parallel on separate features or behaviors, but does not describe combining their analyses into higher-level findings.

r004.rationale: It says agents can handle grunt work so human researchers can focus on judgment and new questions, but does not describe agents moving across abstraction levels to broaden human understanding of a model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that interpretability has a property most research areas don't: the feedback loop is incredibly tight, and it's almost entirely internal to the computer.

If you're doing a biology experiment, you run it, you wait days or weeks, you deal with contamination and noisy instruments. If you're doing interpretability on a neural network, the "organism" is sitting right there in memory. You can ablate a feature, re-run the forward pass, and get an answer in milliseconds. You can read every weight, every activation, every gradient. There's no part of the system that's hidden from you in principle. That means an agent can form a hypothesis, test it, and revise it hundreds of times in the span it would take a human researcher to set up one experiment properly.

The second thing is that a lot of the day-to-day work is honestly grind. You're training sparse autoencoders, sweeping hyperparameters, looking at thousands of features and trying to label what they respond to, checking whether a circuit you found in one layer generalizes to another model. Humans get bored and sloppy doing that at scale. Agents don't, and they can parallelize it. So you can have an agent go look at ten thousand features and flag the hundred that are weird, and then a human spends their time on the hundred rather than the ten thousand.

And the third piece, which I think is underappreciated, is that interpretability is one of the few areas where the agent has a genuine edge in intuition, not just in throughput. These models have some kind of implicit sense of how language models represent things, because they are one. When you ask a strong model to guess what a feature might be doing based on its top activating examples, it's often shockingly good at it, better than a lot of humans, because it's basically doing introspection by proxy.

The caveat I'd add is that this is also where you have to be most careful. An agent studying a model that resembles itself is in a weird epistemic position. You want the verification to be mechanical and reproducible, not "the agent said this circuit does X and it sounded plausible." So the recipe we've found works is: let the agent generate and explore aggressively, but force every claim through automated checks that don't depend on the agent's judgment. When you do that, you get a research loop that moves genuinely faster than any human team could, and you still trust the output.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can form hypotheses, test them through interventions such as ablations, and revise quickly.

r002.rationale: It mentions the scale of feature review, but does not state that a large model’s complexity exceeds what one person can mentally encompass.

r003.rationale: It describes parallelizing feature searches, but not combining analyses of separate model components into higher-level findings.

r004.rationale: It says agents can narrow the workload for humans, but does not describe moving across abstraction levels to help humans gain a broader understanding of a model.

astra-6.text:
I think interpretability is a particularly good fit because so much of the work involves running experiments against a model. You have a hypothesis about what’s happening internally, you write some code to inspect activations or intervene on them, and then you look at whether the results support that hypothesis. That’s a loop an AI agent can potentially execute quite well, because the tools and the thing being studied are both accessible through software.

There’s also a huge search problem. You can find something interesting in one part of a model and then spend a lot of time figuring out which inputs trigger it, what other components it interacts with, and whether it actually matters for the output. Agents could help explore those possibilities much more broadly than a human researcher working alone.

The important distinction, though, is between generating a plausible explanation and testing one. An agent saying, ‘This feature represents deception,’ isn’t enough. You want it to design experiments that could show that interpretation is wrong. If we can build that discipline into the research loop, agents could make interpretability substantially faster while giving humans better evidence to reason from.

r003.rationale: It mentions exploring model components, but does not describe swarms synthesizing separate component analyses into higher-level findings.

r004.rationale: It says agents could help explore possibilities more broadly and give humans better evidence, but does not explain how delegating movement across abstraction levels helps humans understand a model more broadly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think interpretability research has a really useful feedback loop for agents. You can form a hypothesis about what a model is doing, write code to inspect its activations, run an intervention, and see whether the result supports your hypothesis. A lot of that work happens entirely in software, so an agent can move through the whole cycle relatively autonomously.

And there’s a huge amount of exploration involved. A human researcher has limited time to investigate different features, circuits, or examples. Agents can help expand that search and follow up on observations that might otherwise get left behind.

The important distinction is between producing a plausible explanation and actually testing it. If an agent says, “This component is responsible for this behavior,” you want it to intervene on that component and measure what changes. That ability to turn an explanation into an experiment is what makes interpretability such a promising setting.
